One of the biggest things that happened in modern American history is the mutual discovery of tech and government. 

In the 1990s, companies would say, I'm not an American company, I'm a global company, and nowhere was that stronger than in the world of tech, where Google has no boundaries.

Today, tech is actually the locus of international great power competition. 

China's attempt to build a technosphere that can dominate the American technosphere is critical to your business, but also to the American state, to power and independence. 

So much to the surprise of both the tech world and the political world, they've been driven in on each other, and there's a kind of re-nationalization of tech.

If you're a legacy multinational, free trade is the essence of your business. I need financial markets, labor markets, and manufactured good markets that are seamless and open. 

But if you're a tech company, you don't. Google is not importing and exporting a lot of goods. 

You're much more concerned about security of supply chain, security of intellectual property."

I think he made some good points here.

If AI finds a vulnerability in Bitcoin node software or attacks a mining pool, developers can release a patch and node operators/mining pools can update. That doesn't require everyone in Bitcoin to agree on some huge change to the network.

But markets don't wait for patches.

If confidence drops and people start thinking the ecosystem can't be secured anymore, a sell-off happens before any fix goes live.

With quantum computing also becoming a longer-term concern, the industry needs to get ahead of these risks instead of reacting after something breaks.

$BONER pushed the tokenized $HIMS from around $29 to $132 over the weekend.

What's interesting is the actual $HIMS stock itself barely moved.

So now you've got tokenized $HIMS trading 4x above the real thing. The Arb bots are hammering the pool trying to close that gap, degens keep buying against them, and every one of those swaps pays a fee to whoever's providing the liquidity.

When there's that many trades going on, somebody's getting paid. 

And they're doing it without needing to call the top, hold either token, or even care where $HIMS price ended up.

Interested in getting a piece?

@revertfinance currently shows LPs around stocks like RBLX/USDG and HOOD/USDG, alongside all the usual high-volatility crypto pools.

Some of the top positions have completely ridiculous displayed APRs. There's a WETH/FOMO position showing 87K%+ APR right now.

Obviously I wouldn't underwrite anything based on a number like that. A concentrated LP can show an insane APR after a short burst of volume and look completely different tomorrow.

Instead of looking at the pool APR and jumping in, you can open the actual LP positions and see their range, age, PnL, ROI, fee APR and liquidity.

So my process is basically:

Find a stock pool getting real volume
 → Check existing LPs on Revert
 → Compare different fee tiers/ranges
 → Look at how long the position has actually been earning
 → Then decide if the fees are worth the LP risk

I'd rather LP a stock w/ $USDG pair than blindly copy the highest-APR meme LP.

You still get exposure to the volume being created around the meme/stock trade, without choosing to become exit liquidity for a random meme.

One catch though...

The $HIMS move above is the reminder that a tokenized stock isn't actually the stock. When CT decides to run it, it decouples from the real ticker and your "safe" stock LP gets run over like any other pair. 

You're not taking stock risk. You're taking stock risk plus whatever CT decides to do with it.

Revert and @KrystalDeFi both handle the management side after that: moving ranges, collecting/compounding fees, automations and PnL tracking.

Everyone is staring at the token doing 10x and overlooking who's collecting fees from all of them.

LPing can be worth it if @RobinhoodCrypto Chain keeps going this direction.

From the Bitcoin pivot through June 2026, common shares increased by roughly 1.13bn. 60%+ of those came after June 2025 after the stock peaked. 

In fairness to management, as far as I can tell the Series 10 ratchet was disclosed in the March 2024 annual report just days before the Bitcoin pivot, and again in the March 2025 annual report. The April 2024 Bitcoin announcement did not highlight it, and the quarterly/half-year filings appear to have disclosed the outstanding rights but not the 20% ratchet mechanics. (Happy to be corrected here).

We should also concede the history: Simon was running a tiny distressed microcap when Series 10 was designed in...2022? A huge equity incentive in that situation is not that crazy.

So this was not hidden. An investor doing the work could have found it. The trickiness of dealing with Japanese disclosures, despite my fluency in Japanese, thankfully kept me from owning 3350 in any size after we exited that month.

Management also did a good job growing BTC per share. Had they simply tied comp to that, they still could have made $$$ for the accretion. They did their jobs.

Unfortunately, the windfall produced by the 20% ratchet has become grotesque relative to the company’s current market cap and the stock’s performance since the peak, and leaves management imperfectly aligned with shareholders from here.

Disclosure: I bought a little today. The stock is cheap, I'm more bullish on Bitcoin these days and more willing to take varying exposures. It's not so hard, though perhaps personally a bit expensive, to make things right going forward.

i've been grinding hard for over a year now. if you are over 35 years old and have 30+ pounds to lose, here's my advice:

- the first step is understanding that something in your lifestyle is very broken. probably not just one thing, either
- you didn't gain all of that weight in a few months, nor will you lose it in a few months. to make it truly sustainable and fueled by permanent lifestyle changes, adjust your time horizon to 1-2 years
- focus on improving your fitness first rather than losing weight, with a foundation of progressive overload resistance training (lifting  heavy weights to within ~3 reps of failure) at least 2x per week some other activity you enjoy 2x per week (for me it's yoga). make sure you walk long distances on off days, and on every other day that you reasonably can
- spend ~3-4 months building up muscle (especially if you are de-conditioned) before making big changes to your diet
- cook your own meals for 80% to 90% of what you eat. meal prep absolutely works if you don't eat junk snacks in-between meals (look for recipes on YouTube). use AI to create healthy, batch recipes of your favorite foods if needed. cook batches of 6-8 servings and freeze them in high quality containers designed for this purpose. plan out what you will eat in advance the next day
- prioritize protein intake (up to 1 gram per pound of target bodyweight, though i personally do closer to 0.75-0.8 g). don't regularly eat junk carbs (like chips, candy, and cakes). eat only when you are hungry, but try to get 3 meals per day to keep your protein intake consistent
- when you start to lose fat, your appearance might not change much due to muscle backfilling it. you may go ~6 months without noticing any big visual changes. monitor body fat mass vs lean muscle mass using either dexa scan or a well-calibrated impedance sensor scale for directional data
- so instead, focus on your improved fitness, feeling in your body, and how your clothes start to fit. forget the number on the scale. it will drop when it is time
- losing fat is like removing sheets of paper from a roll of paper towels. when there are 100 sheets on there, if you remove one, you can barely see it. when you are down to 10-20 sheets, removing one sheet is noticeable

if you put in the work consistently, and are patient and focus on the right goals (improving your health, and weight loss is just one part of it) then you can achieve your goals

get out there and crush it 💪

A former colleague of mine just shared one of my old business cycle indicators.

I built it. It stayed at Pictet when I left.

Funny thing about rebuilding a process from scratch... it forces you to revisit your old work with a fresh pair of eyes.

I've done it many times now. Every time, there are improvements to be made.

So let me be blunt about this one: it's dead.

It’s a composite. Labor market conditions, the yield curve, the output gap, profit margins, consumer sentiment, wages... roughly fifteen inputs, ranked in percentile.

Many of those inputs have lost their meaning in a K-shaped economy. They were built to read a broad, synchronized cycle, where labor, credit and profits moved together. That economy doesn't exist anymore. So the signal degrades.

You can see it plainly in the chart: the last time this indicator hit the 90th percentile, it should have called a recession. In the old world it would have. This time it didn’t.

The changes I've been writing about for the past eighteen months have broken most of these old-school macro models. Or at the very least, made them far less important than they used to be.

This is exactly why the loud voices calling for recession these past 2-3 years have all been wrong. I took the other side.

I explained why they were wrong... initially in a GMI piece last year, then more completely in one titled The Compute Cycle, one of the last pieces I wrote before I left GMI.

Here's the bigger issue.

Everyone is building dashboards now. AI handed the world a new set of power tools, and almost overnight, anyone could ship a model.

However, AI made it possible for anyone to build tools. What it has not done is make everyone a toolmaker.

The difference is judgment.

Most people have been handed the capability without the apprenticeship.

They can produce the model. They cannot tell you how it works. And if you can't do that, you can't refine it.

The oldest rule in this business does not care how good the technology gets: garbage in, garbage out.

This old chart of mine is not the only one.

The Financial Conditions Index I developed years ago… same story: dying.

Why?

Because the ground underneath these indicators is moving, and fast.

For forty years the business cycle lived inside a cage. That cage held through the dotcom bust, the Global Financial Crisis, COVID, and half a dozen Fed cycles.

Then this year global semiconductor sales posted the largest annual increase in over four decades, and the cage broke.

Compute stopped being a downstream input to the real-world production cycle and became the binding constraint.

Growth now starts with chips and propagates outward. Everything else sits downstream. And that guts the old financial conditions logic.

These frameworks were built for a world where cash flow sensitivity to rates, a strong dollar and high oil prices governed the cycle.

The dollar still matters, it always will, it's the price of global liquidity. Rates and oil still matter too. But their grip on the cycle has loosened.

When capex is funded off corporate balance sheets running a moonshot, and the buildout is a strategic imperative nobody can opt out of (the Red Queen Effect), those old transmission channels matter far less than they used to.

When the causality of the entire cycle flips, the tools built to read the old one don't just need tuning. They need burying.

For well over a decade I've built asset allocation models and business cycle frameworks for some of the most sophisticated investors in the world.

That work, and the discipline of staying relentlessly data-dependent, is what I'm known for.

The craft beneath it has always been the same. Statistics and econometrics. The unglamorous stuff you can't shortcut, and can't fake.

It comes with me on this next venture. A full suite of new indicators, built from the ground up.

I'll be sharing much more in Q4.

The macro landscape is shifting. More now than ever.

Time to sit up...

After reading this, I can’t shake the feeling that we may already be living in a Three-Body world—one in which humanity is gradually, and perhaps inevitably, dividing itself into three camps: the Adventists, the Redemptionists, and the Survivors.

The Adventists want the Trisolarans to come. They see the arrival of a superior intelligence not as an existential threat, but as a potential replacement for a civilization they believe has reached its limits.

The Redemptionists also believe the Trisolarans can save us—but they hope that the two civilizations can coexist, with superior intelligence serving as a means of transcending the flaws of human civilization rather than replacing it.

The Survivors, by contrast, ask a much more primitive question: How do we survive the Trisolarans? For them, the preservation of human agency and human civilization takes precedence over the promise of whatever the future intelligence might bring.

What makes the analogy increasingly unsettling is the rapid emergence of superintelligence.

Perhaps we have already begun to fall, consciously or unconsciously, into these three camps. Some are eagerly anticipating the arrival of something greater than ourselves. Some believe AI will ultimately redeem humanity from many of the constraints that have defined our civilization. And some are increasingly preoccupied with a more fundamental question: whether humans will remain the ones making the decisions in the world we are creating.

The most interesting question, then, may not be whether superintelligence will transform human civilization. That increasingly seems inevitable.

The deeper question is which of these three visions of the future will ultimately prevail—and what happens when the people holding them begin competing for control over the intelligence that will shape that future?

Perhaps the future of AI will be determined not simply by how intelligent machines become, but by the relative dynamics and power of the Adventists, the Redemptionists, and the Survivors among us.
